solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Block off border with sharp spikes (6)

blocks.note: to bar off a road is to block it off
a border is a flower bed along the edge of a garden

annotation.surface: Someone fencing off their garden edge with spiky wire.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Border' looks like a fence-line to go with the spikes; here it is the gardener's border, a bed of flowers.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a barb is a sharp backward-pointing spike, so anything fitted with them, like the wire, fits the description.

entries.clue: Great leader raised new hatchet to cut tree (9)

indicatorNotes.raised: in a down clue, raising a word lifts it upward, reading it bottom to top
indicatorNotes.to cut: the reversed letters cut into the tree, sitting inside it

blocks.note: the ALDER, opened up to take the insert
N is the standard abbreviation for new
a hatchet is a small axe; N + AXE read upward gives EXAN
the rest of ALDER

annotation.surface: A mighty ruler taking a fresh hatchet to a tree.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Great' is part of the definition, not praise: Alexander the Great is the leader meant.
annotation.definitionFit: Alexander the Great led the Macedonian conquest of Persia.

entries.clue: In good spirits, you bat second for once after tossing (7)

indicatorNotes.after tossing: tossing throws the letters of YOU BAT about
indicatorNotes.second for: take the second letter of the word that follows

blocks.note: anagram fodder
the second letter of ONCE

annotation.surface: A cricket captain, cheerful after winning the toss, lets the opposition bat second for a change.
annotation.walkthrough: The cricket picture makes 'tossing' the coin toss and 'second' the batting order; in fact 'tossing' mixes letters and 'second' picks a letter out of 'once'.
annotation.definitionFit: Buoyant means cheerful and optimistic.

entries.clue: Daughters notice chap with an interest in them (3)

annotation.definition: chap with an interest in them

blocks.note: d is the standard abbreviation for daughter(s), as in family trees
an ad is a notice, an advertisement

annotation.surface: Some girls spotting a man who seems keen on them.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an admirer; the 'interest' is the fond concern of a father, and 'them' points back to the daughters.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic-leaning description: a father naturally cares about his own children, with 'them' pointing back to the daughters in the wordplay.

entries.clue: UCAS uncovered shortage, less university space available (8)

indicatorNotes.uncovered: strip the cover, the outer letters, from UCAS
indicatorNotes.less: take away the letter for university

blocks.note: UCAS without its first and last letters
PAUCITY, a shortage, minus U for university

annotation.surface: UCAS, the UK university admissions service, reveals a shortfall in available places.
annotation.walkthrough: UCAS is the body that handles UK university applications, which makes the surface a news headline about places; 'uncovered' here strips the word's outer letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Capacity is the space available, how much something can hold.

entries.clue: Top club, perhaps on island (5)

blocks.note: a club is one suit of playing card; 'perhaps' flags an example
I is the standard abbreviation for island

annotation.surface: Praise for the best nightclub, maybe on some holiday island.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Top club' reads as the best nightclub, but 'Top' is a garment and 'club' a playing card.
annotation.definitionFit: A cardi, short for cardigan, is a knitted top.

entries.clue: Working uptown, crew expanded (3,2,6)

indicatorNotes.Working: the letters of UPTOWN are put to work in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder
a rowing eight is a crew of eight oarsmen

annotation.surface: A work crew in a smart part of town grows larger.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crew' sounds like staff being hired; it is the rowing boat called an eight.
annotation.definitionFit: To put on weight is to expand, grow heavier.

entries.clue: Destructive caterpillar couple fed to dog back on farm (7)

indicatorNotes.fed to: the couple goes inside the dog, like food
indicatorNotes.back on: take the back, the last letter, of FARM

blocks.note: a cur is a mongrel dog, opened up
a couple is two
the rest of CUR
the last letter of FARM

annotation.surface: A farm dog being fed a pair of pests.
annotation.walkthrough: The farm scene fits the pest; the cutworm is a moth caterpillar that chews seedlings through at the base.
annotation.definitionFit: Cutworms are caterpillars that cut young plants off at ground level.

entries.clue: Figure of speech in telegraphist’s last cable (5)

indicatorNotes.last: take the final letter of TELEGRAPHIST

blocks.note: the last letter of TELEGRAPHIST
a cable is a thick rope

annotation.surface: A turn of phrase in the final telegram a telegraph operator sent.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cable' sits in a telegraph clue so it reads as a telegram; it is the thick rope.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from rhetoric, where the word covers any figurative turn such as metaphor or irony.

entries.clue: Part-time judge dealing with injunction catches cold (8)

indicatorNotes.catches: the phrase built from RE + ORDER catches C inside it

blocks.note: re means concerning, dealing with
C for cold, as on taps
an injunction is a court order

annotation.surface: A judge handling a court injunction while nursing a cold.
annotation.walkthrough: In England and Wales a recorder is a barrister or solicitor who sits as a judge part-time, so the legal surface is also the answer's world.
annotation.definitionFit: A British legal title: in England and Wales, practising lawyers sit as judges for a few weeks a year under this name.

entries.clue: Art one suffers for — bric-a-brac likewise? (6)

blocks.note: tat is cheap junk, bric-a-brac
too means also, likewise

annotation.surface: A wry aside that suffering for your art applies to cheap ornaments as well.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Suffering for one's art' is usually a figure of speech; with a tattoo the suffering is the needle.
annotation.definitionFit: A tattoo is body art that hurts to acquire.

entries.clue: German agreed, maniac in novel is wrecking story (7,3)

indicatorNotes.novel: novel as an adjective means new, so the letters of MANIAC IN take a new form

blocks.note: ja is German for yes
anagram fodder

annotation.surface: A German agrees that a madman in a novel is ruining the story.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Novel' seems to name the book; it is an anagram indicator. The story is Daphne du Maurier's Cornish tale of wreckers who lure ships onto rocks.
annotation.definitionFit: Jamaica Inn is du Maurier's novel about a gang of ship-wreckers.

entries.clue: Burn carbon on standard tariff (11)

blocks.note: C is the chemical symbol for carbon
used as itself
a standard is a flag
a tariff is a rate charged

annotation.surface: Burning carbon billed at the ordinary energy tariff.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Standard tariff' reads as a single utility phrase; it splits into two separate pieces, FLAG and RATE.
annotation.definitionFit: A rare but plain synonym, the verb behind conflagration, a great fire.

entries.clue: Poem for recital not settled yet (4)

indicatorNotes.for recital: a recital is spoken out loud, so take the sound

blocks.note: an ode is a poem

annotation.surface: A poem meant for performance whose words are still not final.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Settled' reads as a draft being finalised; it is a bill being paid.
annotation.definitionFit: Money still due on an unpaid bill: a debt not yet settled is outstanding.

entries.clue: Tied in knots, prepare for release (4)

indicatorNotes.in knots: letters tied in knots are tangled out of order

blocks.note: anagram fodder

annotation.surface: Someone bound up in knots getting ready to be freed.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'release' freedom from bonds; it is the release of a book or film.
annotation.definitionFit: Editing a text or film prepares it for publication.

entries.clue: Bottom section of genuine Thermos twists (10)

indicatorNotes.section of: the answer is a section of the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of 'genuine', through 'Thermos', to the first letter of 'twists'

annotation.surface: The base of a real vacuum flask screws on.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Twists' looks like an anagram indicator for Thermos; it only supplies the final T.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain, rather archaic synonym for lowest, built on 'nether' as in the nether regions.

entries.clue: Bonus / point (3)

blocks.note: extra money given for good service
the pointed end of something

annotation.walkthrough: The slash in the printed clue marks the split between the two definitions.
annotation.definitionFit: A tip is a gratuity, a bonus; it is also a point, as in the tip of a pen.

entries.clue: Penny cracking cryptic clues had to guess (9)

indicatorNotes.cracking: the penny breaks into the jumbled clues
indicatorNotes.cryptic: the letters of CLUES are written in a cryptic, disguised order

blocks.note: first letter of SECUL, an anagram of CLUES
p is a penny
the rest of SECUL
to have a meal is to eat, so had = ate

annotation.surface: A solver whose penny hasn't dropped, forced to guess at cryptic clues.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is the solver's own experience; 'had' is ate, as in having dinner.
annotation.definitionFit: To speculate is to guess without firm evidence.

entries.clue: Might forager bring home the bacon, after taking this out? (7,3)

annotation.definition: Might forager bring home the bacon, after taking this out?

blocks.clueFragment: Might forager bring home the bacon
blocks.note: the surface reading: would a foraging animal earn its keep? 'Bring home the bacon' is an idiom for earning a living
the setter's reading: remove the first word of the answer's name and what is left is literally a pig, the source of bacon

annotation.surface: A question about whether a foraging animal would still earn its keep once something is removed.
annotation.walkthrough: A truffle pig is a forager that finds truffles; take TRUFFLE out of its name and PIG is left, which is literally bacon. 'Bring home the bacon' means earn a living.
annotation.definitionFit: Truffle pigs are used to sniff out and dig up truffles.

entries.clue: Loud blowing to cool food down? (7)

blocks.note: to fan something is to cool it
fare is food
surface padding that also nods to this being a down entry, FAN above FARE

annotation.surface: Blowing hard on a hot dish to cool it before eating.
annotation.walkthrough: The blowing looks like breath over hot food; it is trumpets. 'Down' just places FAN above FARE in this down entry.
annotation.definitionFit: A fanfare is a loud flourish blown on trumpets.

entries.clue: How much fun this is? Very little, you’d say (4)

indicatorNotes.you’d say: said out loud, one word sounds like another

blocks.note: wee is Scottish and British for very small

annotation.surface: A dry reply to a question about how enjoyable something is: hardly at all.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the exclamation itself: 'whee!' is what you say when having fun, so 'this' is the word.
annotation.definitionFit: Whee is a cry of delight, how you express fun.

entries.clue: Test team declines after success (7)

blocks.note: a win is a success
to die away is to decline

annotation.surface: A sports side that fades after winning.
annotation.walkthrough: The Windies is the nickname of the West Indies cricket team, which plays Test (five-day international) matches; 'declines' also sounds like a cricket declaration.
annotation.definitionFit: The Windies are the West Indies, a Test-playing cricket nation.

entries.clue: Man advancing by single steps north on foot (4)

blocks.note: a paw is an animal's foot
N is the abbreviation for north; placed after PAW

annotation.surface: A man walking north step by step.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Man' is a chess piece, and a pawn moves one square at a time; 'north on foot' puts N after PAW in an across answer.
annotation.definitionFit: In chess the pawn is a man that advances one square at a time.

entries.clue: Mud bricks are good enough in Lincoln? (5)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places the phrase for 'good enough' inside the name that Lincoln stands for

blocks.note: ABE, Abraham Lincoln's nickname, opened up
'that will do' means it is good enough
the rest of ABE

annotation.surface: Asking whether mud bricks would pass muster in the English city of Lincoln.
annotation.walkthrough: Lincoln looks like the English cathedral city; it is Abraham Lincoln, US president, known as Abe.
annotation.definitionFit: Adobe is sun-dried mud brick.

entries.clue: Ice creams in Rome? We in Paris like jelly (10)

blocks.note: gelati is Italian for ice creams
nous is French for we

annotation.surface: A tourist compares Roman ice cream to a Parisian's liking for jelly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Like' reads as the verb, the French liking jelly; it belongs to the definition and means resembling.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word comes from gelatine, the setting agent in jelly.

entries.clue: Regretful having traded small for large vehicle (5)

indicatorNotes.having traded: one letter is swapped for another
indicatorNotes.for: S is given up in exchange for L

blocks.note: S for small, as on clothing labels: the letter given up from SORRY
L for large, as on clothing labels, takes the S's place at the front
SORRY, regretful, after its S is traded away

annotation.surface: Someone sorry for trading in a small car for a bigger one.
annotation.walkthrough: S and L are the clothing-size abbreviations for small and large; in SORRY the S becomes L. A lorry is a truck.
annotation.definitionFit: A lorry is a large goods vehicle, a truck.

entries.clue: Moonlight, say, really a result of sunlight reflected (6)

indicatorNotes.reflected: a reflection shows things back to front

blocks.note: 'so good' means really good
used as itself
a suntan

annotation.surface: Moonlight explained as really being sunlight bounced back off the moon.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface's science is true, which disguises 'Moonlight' as Beethoven's Moonlight Sonata; 'say' flags it as an example.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Beethoven's Piano Sonata No 14 is nicknamed the Moonlight.

entries.clue: Playwright having Jack return with different giant (8)

indicatorNotes.different: the letters of GIANT made different

blocks.note: jack and tar are both old words for a sailor
anagram fodder

annotation.surface: A dramatist rewriting Jack and the Beanstalk with Jack coming back and a new giant.
annotation.walkthrough: Jack and the giant call up the fairy tale; Jack is a sailor, TAR. Terence Rattigan was a British playwright (The Winslow Boy).
annotation.definitionFit: Terence Rattigan wrote plays such as The Browning Version.

entries.clue: Pet that won’t get pregnant until married (3)

blocks.note: from nine to five = from nine until five
m is the abbreviation for married

annotation.surface: A prim rule that a pet should not become pregnant before marriage.
annotation.walkthrough: The moral tone is the joke; a tom is a male cat, which can never get pregnant.
annotation.definitionFit: A tom is a male cat, a pet that cannot be pregnant.

entries.clue: Measure yard next to church; ie the churchyard (8)

indicatorNotes.next to: the church abbreviation sits right beside the measure and yard, ahead of them

annotation.definitionNote: 'the churchyard' names one burial ground, as the answer is used with an article

blocks.note: CE is the Church of England
a meter measures, as a gas meter does
y is the abbreviation for yard

annotation.surface: A surveyor measuring the yard beside a church, which is to say the churchyard.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue seems to define itself twice over; 'yard' is really just the letter Y, and 'measure' uses the US spelling of the device that measures.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a churchyard is the burial ground around a church, and the answer is any burial ground.

entries.clue: Miles one travels across snow, given wrong directions (6)

blocks.note: m is the abbreviation for miles
I is the Roman numeral one
to sled is to travel by sledge

annotation.surface: A long snowy trek made after being pointed the wrong way.
annotation.walkthrough: SLED is the verb here, past tense of travelling on a sledge, which is how 'travels' fits.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past participle: led astray, pointed the wrong way.
